title: ChatGPT-5 in Secondary Education: A Mixed-Methods Analysis of Student Attitudes, AI Anxiety, and Hallucination-Aware Use
extended_summary:
This paper examines how secondary school students perceive and use ChatGPT-5 in formal education, with particular attention to attitudes toward AI, AI-related anxiety, and how students respond to hallucinated or inaccurate AI outputs. The study addresses gaps in the GenAI-in-education literature by focusing on high school students rather than university populations, by reporting specific interaction modalities used during the intervention, and by explicitly exposing students to hallucinations to study how they manage accuracy concerns.

The intervention was embedded in the Greek national curriculum course “Technology” and took place over three days in three Greek high schools. A total of 109 sixteen-year-old students participated in an approximately eight-hour classroom intervention. Students used ChatGPT-5 across several modalities and tasks, including information seeking, CV generation, document summarization, video summarization, image generation, quiz generation, and age-adapted explanations. A central feature of the intervention was deliberate exposure to hallucinated outputs: students were shown pre-identified incorrect responses, asked the chatbot the same questions, and then checked the correct answers. Quantitative data came from the SATAI and AIAS scales, and qualitative data came from semi-structured interviews with 36 students.

The study found that students held moderately positive attitudes toward AI overall, with stronger cognitive and affective views than behavioral intentions. Students generally believed AI was important and useful, but were less likely to express intentions to pursue AI-related careers or extracurricular engagement. AI anxiety was moderate overall, with relatively modest learning-related anxiety but stronger concerns about AI-driven dependence, laziness, and human replacement. Female students reported significantly more positive cognitive attitudes than males, while prior ChatGPT users showed more favorable attitudes across all SATAI dimensions. Attitudes and anxiety were essentially uncorrelated.

Qualitative findings identified four main affordances: knowledge expansion, immediate feedback, a familiar interface, and perceived skill development. Three key constraints were also reported: uncertainty about content accuracy, anxiety related to AI feedback, and privacy concerns. A notable contribution of the paper is the concept of “epistemic safeguarding,” describing how students, after encountering hallucinations, restricted AI use to topics where they already had enough prior knowledge to verify answers. The paper concludes that effective GenAI integration in secondary education requires not only access to AI tools but also explicit support for critical AI literacy and hallucination-aware use.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot / large language model used for conversational text generation and multimodal tasks such as summarization, explanation, quiz generation, and image generation.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in an 8-hour secondary school intervention in the Greek 'Technology' course for information seeking, CV generation, document and video summarization, image generation via DALL-E, student-generated quizzes, age-adapted explanations, and deliberate exposure to hallucinated outputs.

findings.finding_summary: Across 109 secondary students, SATAI results showed moderately positive attitudes toward GenAI overall (Total SATAI M=3.24, SD=0.79), with higher cognitive (M=3.44, SD=0.71) and affective attitudes (M=3.38, SD=0.80) than behavioral intentions (M=3.04, SD=1.01). Prior ChatGPT users reported more positive attitudes than non-users on total SATAI (M=3.57 vs. 3.09; t(68.48)=3.13, p=.003, d=0.63), cognitive (t(62.02)=2.82, p=.007, d=0.59), affective (t(61.02)=3.31, p=.002, d=0.70), and behavioral scores (t(70.84)=2.35, p=.021, d=0.47).
findings.measure: Student Attitude Towards Artificial Intelligence scale (SATAI) total and subscales

findings.finding_summary: Students reported moderate AI anxiety overall, with lower learning-related anxiety (AIAS Learning M=3.09, SD=1.37) and higher concern about job replacement (AIAS Job Replacement M=4.07, SD=1.66). Gender differences in anxiety were small and non-significant for total AIAS (M_male=3.58, M_female=3.36; t(87.45)=0.82, p=.416, d=0.16), and attitudes and anxiety were essentially uncorrelated (total SATAI vs. total AIAS: r=-.05, p=.60).
findings.measure: Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS) total, learning anxiety, and job replacement anxiety; correlation between SATAI and AIAS

findings.finding_summary: Female students reported significantly more positive cognitive attitudes toward AI than male students (M=3.68 vs. 3.09; t(95.23)=-4.71, p<.001, d=-0.91, partial η²=.19), with a smaller significant difference on total SATAI (M=3.35 vs. 3.06; t(101.12)=-1.99, p=.049, d=-0.38). Affective and behavioral differences also favored female students but were not statistically significant.
findings.measure: SATAI by gender: total, cognitive, affective, behavioral subscales

findings.finding_summary: Qualitative interviews with 36 students identified four perceived affordances of ChatGPT: generating new knowledge (N=29), immediate feedback (N=18), friendly/familiar interface (N=16), and skill development including computational thinking, problem-solving, critical thinking, and digital literacy (N=10). Students often reported using ChatGPT to clarify partially understood concepts rather than replace instruction.

After experiencing hallucinated outputs, many students reported restricting future ChatGPT use to topics where they already had enough prior knowledge to verify responses, which the author terms 'epistemic safeguarding.' Interviews also identified constraints around uncertainty about content accuracy (N=21), anxiety related to AI feedback (N=11), and privacy/data protection concerns (N=4).
findings.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on hallucination-aware use and constraints

quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods primary study with descriptive statistics, subgroup comparisons, and qualitative interviews, but no randomized control group or causal design estimating learning effects. Evidence is useful but remains observational/intervention-based with limited causal credibility.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows meaningful attitudinal differences and identifies notable anxiety and critical-use patterns, but outcomes are mostly perceptions, attitudes, and qualitative themes rather than direct academic achievement gains. Impact on learning is therefore suggestive but unclear.
